title: Polynomial-time density learning of Gaussian mixtures
formal: Does there exist a uniform randomized algorithm that properly learns every mixture of at most \(k\) nondegenerate Gaussian distributions on \(\mathbb R^d\), to any fixed total-variation accuracy, in time polynomial jointly in \(k\) and \(d\)? Precisely, is there one algorithm \(A\) in the arithmetic model below such that, for every integer \(t\ge3\), there are integers \(C_t,a_t\ge1\) for which the following holds for all integers \(k,d\ge1\) and all \(P\in\mathcal G_{k,d}\)? Given \(k,d,t\) and independent samples from \(P\), the algorithm uses at most \(C_t(k+d)^{a_t}\) operations and outputs a description of \(\widehat P\in\mathcal G_{k,d}\) satisfying \[\Pr[d_{\mathrm{TV}}(P,\widehat P)\le1/t]\ge2/3.\] The time bound holds on every execution and includes sampling and writing the output. Its constants are uniform over all mixture parameters. No polynomial dependence on \(t\) is required: this card asks the source's joint polynomial dependence on the number of components and dimension at each fixed accuracy.

source_formulation.text: Can Gaussian mixtures be learned in running time polynomial in both the number of components and the ambient dimension, even without privacy?
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of the source question on page 6

why: Gaussian mixtures are a basic example where enough observations can be available but extracting a useful distribution from them may remain computationally difficult. Joint dependence on dimension and component count distinguishes scalable learning from methods efficient only for a small fixed mixture. Resolving this target would clarify that statistical–computational gap in the absence of separation or conditioning assumptions.
status_note: Source-open in ALT 2024 for joint polynomial dependence on component count and dimension. On 16 September 2026 the full source definitions and question, the 2017 and 2022 hardness manuscripts, the November 2024 score-matching theorem, and the April 2025/August 2026 primary abstracts were checked. A bounded later-work search found no unconditional resolution of the stated target. Proper output follows the source definition; fixed-accuracy quantifiers and exact-real primitives are explicit editorial computational conventions, not a claimed bit-complexity theorem. Conditional hardness and restricted-model lower bounds remain qualified. Cited proofs were not independently verified or formalized in Lean.

progress.text: Diakonikolas–Kane–Stewart establish statistical-query obstacles to general Gaussian-mixture density estimation.
Gupte–Vafa–Vaikuntanathan strengthen conditional density-estimation hardness using reductions from Learning with Errors.
Afzali–Ashtiani–Liaw obtain polynomial sample sufficiency under privacy and explicitly retain efficient joint dependence on component count and dimension as a question even without privacy.
The second score-matching manuscript version gives a sampler with a dimension exponent depending on component count and accuracy, under its bounded-parameter assumptions.
Parallel-pancake work supplies additional statistical-query lower bounds and a restricted quasipolynomial testing result.
A work-in-progress manuscript claims sharp proper estimation for fixed-component, bounded-mean, unit-covariance mixtures.

category_assignment.reason: The selected passage explicitly asks efficient nonprivate Gaussian-mixture density learning, even though its paper establishes a private sample bound.

importance.reason: A central statistical–computational question for a widely used distribution family: polynomial sample sufficiency contrasts with strong restricted-model and conditional hardness evidence. The unconstrained joint dependence is substantially broader than fixed-component or separated-mixture algorithms; the score concerns this density-learning target, not every private-learning problem in the source.

sentences: The learner receives independent observations from a mixture of at most k nondegenerate Gaussians in d dimensions.
It must output another such mixture whose whole distribution is close in total variation, without reconstructing the original components.
The question asks for a uniform algorithm with time polynomial jointly in k and d for each fixed accuracy, using explicitly specified exact-real arithmetic.
Polynomial sample sufficiency coexists with statistical-query lower bounds and conditional computational hardness, neither of which is silently treated as an unconditional resolution.
Newer positive results with bounded parameters, fixed component counts or growing dimension exponents do not establish the full target.

definitions: For a positive integer \(d\), a nondegenerate Gaussian distribution \(N(\mu,\Sigma)\) has mean \(\mu\in\mathbb R^d\) and a symmetric positive-definite matrix \(\Sigma\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}\). Positive definite means \(v^{\mathsf T}\Sigma v>0\) for every nonzero \(v\in\mathbb R^d\). Its density at \(x\in\mathbb R^d\) is \[(2\pi)^{-d/2}(\det\Sigma)^{-1/2}\exp\!\left(-\tfrac12(x-\mu)^{\mathsf T}\Sigma^{-1}(x-\mu)\right).\] The class \(\mathcal G_{k,d}\) consists of all distributions \(P=\sum_{i=1}^k w_iN(\mu_i,\Sigma_i)\), where \(w_i\ge0\), \(\sum_iw_i=1\), and each component satisfies the preceding conditions. Zero weights allow fewer than \(k\) components; repeated components are allowed. Means, covariance eigenvalues and component separation have no upper or lower promises beyond positive definiteness, and positive weights have no prescribed minimum. If \(p,q\) are the densities of \(P,Q\), their total variation distance is \[d_{\mathrm{TV}}(P,Q)=\tfrac12\int_{\mathbb R^d}|p(x)-q(x)|\,dx,\] where integration is with respect to Lebesgue measure. The learner has no access to the hidden component label or parameters. Each sampling request returns a fresh independent vector drawn from \(P\). The output consists of \(k\) weights, \(k\) means and \(k\) positive-definite covariance matrices, describing a valid member of the same class on every execution. This requirement is called proper learning. No correspondence between true and output components is required. The success probability is over all sampled vectors and the algorithm's independent fair random bits. Computational convention: \(A\) is one finite program, with rational constants and no nonuniform advice, using exact real registers together with a Turing work tape. Allowed real operations are copying, addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by a nonzero value, square root of a nonnegative value, and order or equality comparisons; each costs one operation. Reading or writing a real register costs one operation; a sample vector costs \(d\) operations. Each fair random bit and each ordinary tape step costs one operation. Integer inputs use binary encoding. Undefined arithmetic operations are forbidden. Each output scalar must be written and charged. No integration, optimization, density-evaluation or arbitrary-function oracle is available. The density formula defines the mathematical distribution, not an extra primitive of the program. This explicit arithmetic convention measures computation on real observations; it does not claim polynomial bit complexity for an unspecified finite-precision encoding.
answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-checked proof of the algorithm-existence statement or of its logical negation in the stated model. An affirmative proof must establish validity of the proper output, total execution bound and uniform total-variation guarantee for every allowed mixture and every accuracy parameter. A negative proof must rule out all algorithms in the specified arithmetic model, rather than only statistical-query algorithms or one proposed method. A conditional hardness theorem must be identified with its additional hypothesis and does not by itself settle this unconditional yes/no target. Learning with a fixed number of components, recovering component parameters under separation assumptions, or returning only an arbitrary sampler does not establish the requested statement. The reciprocal-accuracy parameter belongs to the learning guarantee; it is not a single numerical answer to be approximated at the benchmark's default tolerance.

context_blocks.text: A mixture combines several Gaussian populations without telling the learner which population generated an observation. Density learning asks for a distribution that predicts the whole population well. Two different lists of components can describe the same, or nearly the same, distribution; therefore success does not require reconstructing the original list.

The source defines proper PAC learning and unbounded positive-definite Gaussian components. Its highlighted computational question appears in a paper about private learning, but explicitly remains a question even when privacy is removed. The present target has no privacy requirement.

Section 9.3 recalls near-optimal nonprivate sample complexity \(\widetilde\Theta(kd^2/\alpha^2)\) at accuracy \(\alpha\), with logarithmic factors suppressed. A statistical existence bound does not make the search for a suitable mixture polynomial-time. The private construction also uses a nonconstructive cover, a separate obstacle discussed on page 6.

The statement fixes proper output, exact arithmetic primitives and the order of quantifiers explicitly. The source says polynomial in the two structural parameters and does not specify a bit model in its open-question sentence. Allowing the exponent to depend on fixed accuracy avoids silently strengthening that sentence to a fully polynomial accuracy guarantee.

Statistical-query lower bounds restrict algorithms that obtain information through approximate expectations of bounded test functions. They explain an obstruction for a broad family of learning methods, but alone do not exclude every algorithm with direct sample access.

There is also conditional evidence beyond statistical queries. Gupte–Vafa–Vaikuntanathan derive hardness of Gaussian-mixture density estimation from Learning with Errors assumptions. Those assumptions concern the difficulty of recovering or distinguishing hidden linear structure from noisy modular observations. The reductions and computational assumptions belong to their stated model; the card does not promote them to an unconditional theorem for its exact-real machine.

The score-matching theorem assumes a bounded conditioning/size parameter \(\tau\) and minimum positive weight at least inverse-polynomial in \(k\). It uses \(d^{\operatorname{poly}(k\tau/\alpha)}\) samples, runs in time polynomial in that sample count, and returns a sampler. The dimension exponent grows with the number of components, so this guarantee does not supply the joint polynomial bound sought here.

The 2025 parallel-pancake work studies shared-covariance structure and gives statistical-query limitations even with uniform weights, alongside a quasipolynomial testing guarantee. Its restrictions and model remain explicit.

The August 2026 manuscript concerns unit covariances, bounded means and a fixed component count. Its claimed sharp polynomial-time risk bound for that family does not settle arbitrary covariances or joint polynomial dependence. The card records the claim and its scope without asserting independent verification of the manuscript.
